title: Skin lesion classification from smartphone-quality images
summary: A melanoma classifier trained on 400,000 lesions where only 343 were malignant, combining an ensemble of CNNs with clinical metadata.

sections.heading: The problem
body: Skin cancer is usually curable if caught early, and often fatal if it isn't. The bottleneck is access: dermatologists are scarce, and most people don't get a lesion looked at until it's obvious. A model that works on ordinary photographs rather than specialist dermoscopy could triage lesions where no dermatologist is available.
list: Images are 15x15mm tiles cropped from 3D total body photography, closer to smartphone photos than to clinical dermoscopy, each paired with clinical metadata: age, sex, anatomical site, morphometric and colour measurements.
~400,000 benign lesions against 343 malignant ones.
At that ratio a model that predicts "benign" every time is right 99.9% of the time and clinically useless.

images.alt: Illustration of the dataset's label structure: strong-labelled tiles each carrying a specific diagnosis (melanoma invasive, nevus, basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, solar or actinic keratosis) above weak-labelled tiles all marked only as Benign, NOS
images.caption: The same imbalance seen from the label side: a small set of lesions carries a specific confirmed diagnosis, while the bulk are labelled only "Benign, NOS", not otherwise specified.

sections.heading: Approach
body: Three things dealt with the imbalance, and they had to work together:
list: Weighted sampler: oversamples malignant cases, with a fixed 4,000 samples per epoch so batches stay roughly balanced.

Stronger augmentation on the malignant class: oversampling alone shows the model the same 343 images repeatedly, so heavier crops, rotations, colour jitter and erasing generate variety rather than repetition.
Loss weighting handled the rest.
Backbones pretrained on ISIC 2019/2020 9-class data rather than ImageNet, as those already encode pigment networks, border irregularity and vascular structure.
Each backbone frozen, with only a new binary head trained on top: with 343 positives, fine-tuning a full backbone would have overfitted almost immediately.
The head used five parallel dropout branches averaged at output, as a further regulariser.

images.alt: Image preprocessing pipeline: patient-level train/validation/test split before any augmentation, then a deliberately mild augmentation policy with random erasing as regularisation
images.caption: Patient-level split happens before augmentation, not after. The augmentation policy itself stays deliberately mild (no elastic warps or extreme rotations, since dermoscopic structure is the diagnostic signal), then dialled up further for the malignant class specifically.

list: Thirty CNNs total: EfficientNet B4-B7, ResNeSt101 and SE-ResNeXt101, five folds each.
Separately, four models on the metadata alone: MLP, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost.

images.alt: Metadata preprocessing pipeline: diagnosis-derived and high-cardinality columns removed, patient-grouped split, then median imputation and scaling for numeric features, most-frequent imputation and one-hot encoding for categorical ones
images.caption: The metadata pipeline gets the same leakage safeguards as the images: diagnosis-derived and high-cardinality columns dropped before the patient-grouped split, then standard imputation and scaling for the four metadata models.

list: Folds grouped by patient, so no patient appears in both train and validation; otherwise the model can recognise a person rather than a lesion.
Diagnosis-derived columns removed (lesion identifiers, thickness, mitotic index, existing DNN scores), since they would be unavailable at prediction time.
The 30 CNNs collapsed into three signals by averaging within each architecture family, plus one averaged metadata signal.
Those four fed a logistic regression trained on a small held-out set no base model had seen, keeping the meta-model to four inputs and a linear form.

images.alt: Ensemble architecture: 30 CNNs (five EfficientNet variants plus ResNeSt101, five folds each) and four metadata models, both branches producing predictions that feed a logistic regression meta-learner for the final prediction
images.caption: The full stack: image and metadata branches each produce out-of-fold predictions, collapsed to one signal per branch, then combined by a 4-input logistic regression, simple enough to leave little room to overfit on the small held-out set.

sections.heading: Result
list: 0.961 AUC on the private leaderboard, against 0.968 on validation.
The 0.007 gap indicates the validation setup held: the patient-grouped folds and the removed diagnosis-proxy columns did their job.

At the default 0.5 cutoff, 47 of 70 malignant cases caught (67% recall) with 5 false alarms across 430 benign ones (99% specificity), a threshold worth revisiting depending on whether deployment favours catching more malignant cases or fewer false alarms.
The logistic regression coefficients give interpretability for free: image features contribute roughly 52% of the prediction and metadata 48%, so neither source dominates.

images.alt: ROC curve for the final ensemble on the validation set, AUC 0.9689
images.caption: Validation ROC curve for the final ensemble. The 0.969 AUC matches the 0.968 reported above.

images.alt: Confusion matrix at a 0.5 threshold: 425 true negatives, 5 false positives, 23 false negatives, 47 true positives
images.caption: Confusion matrix at the default 0.5 threshold: 67% recall, 99% specificity. Moving the threshold trades one for the other.

sections.heading: Explainability
body: Two checks on what the models were learning, beyond the leaderboard score:
list: Grad-CAM: on the same lesion, EfficientNet B5 concentrates on the core while B7 spreads across both irregular lobes. Backbones attending to different regions is the decorrelated error the ensemble exists to exploit.
Embedding PCA: malignant lesions separate from the benign cluster before the classification head sees them, consistent with fine-tuning the head alone being enough.

images.alt: Grad-CAM heatmap on lesion ISIC_2480600 for EfficientNet B5, attention concentrated on the lesion's core
images.caption: Grad-CAM (pytorch-grad-cam) on the same lesion, one backbone each: B5 settles on a single dense core, B7 splits across both lobes. Where they disagree is the point: averaging models that read the image differently is what the ensemble is for.

images.alt: Grad-CAM heatmap on the same lesion ISIC_2480600 for EfficientNet B7, attention spread across two separate regions
images.caption: Grad-CAM (pytorch-grad-cam) on the same lesion, one backbone each: B5 settles on a single dense core, B7 splits across both lobes. Where they disagree is the point: averaging models that read the image differently is what the ensemble is for.

images.alt: PCA projection of the frozen backbone's embeddings to two components, coloured by malignancy score, showing malignant lesions separating from the benign cluster
images.caption: Frozen-backbone embeddings, projected to two principal components (scikit-learn PCA) and coloured by malignancy score. The separation is visible even at 2D, before the classification head.
